# The Fairhaven corridor: does terminal capital buy throughput?

> A capacity and cost reading of the Fairhaven freight corridor for a committee that has to vote before the October window closes.
> Prepared by: Alexandria
> 28 July 2026

## Executive summary

Northgate Terminals should submit a scoped reception-road proposal in the 2026 funding window and hold the larger scheme back until the corridor's track constraint is settled. The demand case is sound. The throughput case is not, because the limit on how much freight the corridor can move sits on the running line at Ashcombe rather than at the terminal gate.

Corridor freight volume rose from 4.1 million tonnes in 2021 to 6.8 million tonnes in 2025, a gain of two thirds in four years. That growth is recorded by the body that meters the traffic and it is repeated, from the same meters, in local reporting ([Fairhaven Transport Authority, Corridor Access Charge Review 2026](https://example.com/fta/corridor-access-charge-review-2026); [Ravensmoor Gazette](https://gazette.example/ravensmoor/port-rail-volumes-2026)). A committee can plan against it.

What the growth cannot tell a committee is where the next tonne would go. For 11.4 km between Ashcombe Junction and Marleigh the corridor narrows to a single track, and the working timetable sells four freight paths per hour in each direction ([Corridor Access Charge Review 2026](https://example.com/fta/corridor-access-charge-review-2026)). Those paths are sold. A terminal that can accept more trains than the line can deliver has bought a queue.

The operator's own review reports punctuality falling to 82 per cent in 2025 from 91 per cent in 2022, and places the loss on services crossing Ashcombe ([Meridian Freight Rail, Operating and Financial Review 2025](https://example.org/meridian/operating-review-2025)). Read together, the path allocation and the punctuality record point at the single-track section rather than at the terminals: the corridor sells all four hourly paths, and the delay is concentrated where trains must wait for each other. That is analysis rather than a measurement, and the section below states what would overturn it.

The cost side is unsettled in a way the committee should price as a range rather than a number. The operator puts the increase at 4.2 million pounds a year from the 2027 period ([Operating and Financial Review 2025](https://example.org/meridian/operating-review-2025)). The authority's review puts the same increase at 2.6 million pounds a year across all corridor operators ([Corridor Access Charge Review 2026](https://example.com/fta/corridor-access-charge-review-2026)). Neither party has published the bridge between the two figures, and the difference is large enough to move a payback calculation by more than a year.

One piece of evidence cuts against the constraint finding, and it deserves to be read before the recommendation rather than after it. Calderbank's assessment found four of the twenty-eight night paths across the section unused in the autumn 2025 timetable, which is the strongest evidence against treating the track as full ([Calderbank Rail Engineering, Ashcombe Section Capacity Assessment](https://example.net/calderbank/ashcombe-capacity-assessment)). If loaded trains can use those paths, the corridor has room the daytime figures hide, and the case for spending capital weakens to a resilience argument.

The recommendation therefore has two parts. Submit now, because the authority's investment committee opens one window a year and a missed window costs a full charge period. Phase the scheme, because the evidence that would justify the second phase does not exist yet and can be obtained cheaply through a night-path trial.

## What the corridor is, and why the question arises now

The Fairhaven corridor is the 62 km rail link between Ashcombe Junction, where traffic joins from the national network, and the deep-water berths at Ravensmoor Port. It carries bulk aggregates, containerised imports moving inland, and a growing share of palletised retail freight that used to travel by road. Northgate Terminals operates the inland interchange at Marleigh, roughly two thirds of the way along the corridor, and the question in front of its investment committee is narrow: whether to fund a second reception road at that interchange in the 2026 funding window.

The question arises now for two reasons that are unrelated to each other. The first is that the authority has opened its periodic access charge review, which will set the price of using the corridor for the five years from 2027. The second is that the interchange at Marleigh has been running at its practical limit on weekday afternoons for about eighteen months, and the operating team has asked for relief.

Those two facts pull in opposite directions. A charge review is a reason to wait, because the price of the traffic the terminal would serve is not yet known. An interchange at its limit is a reason to move, because a reception road takes about fourteen months to build and commission. The committee cannot resolve the tension by preference. It has to decide which of the two constraints actually binds the flow of freight, and that is an evidentiary question rather than a matter of taste.

This report answers that question and states the confidence behind each part of the answer. It separates what the record establishes, what the parties assert about each other's costs, and what is inference drawn by the analyst. Where the evidence runs out, the report says so rather than filling the space.

The reader is a committee of five that meets monthly and votes on capital above a threshold. Its members are not railway engineers. They will not read a working timetable, and they should not have to. What they need is the shape of the constraint, the range of the cost, and the two or three facts that would make them change their minds.

That audience shapes what this report includes. Track geometry appears only where it changes the answer. Charge mechanics appear only to the depth needed to understand why two competent parties can publish figures that differ by 1.6 million pounds a year. The governance timetable appears because it sets a deadline the committee cannot move.

### The corridor in its regional setting

The corridor does not exist in isolation, and two features of its surroundings bear on the committee's decision.

The first is the port. Ravensmoor's deep-water berths are the reason containerised traffic exists on this line at all, and port throughput sets the ceiling on that flow. A port that grows its container volumes pushes more boxes inland; a port that loses a shipping line pushes fewer. The corridor's second-largest commodity flow is therefore hostage to commercial decisions taken by parties who have no interest in the corridor's timetable. That is not a reason to avoid investing, but it is a reason to prefer a scheme whose value does not depend on that flow growing.

The second is the road network the corridor competes with. Palletised retail freight is the flow that has grown fastest, and it is the flow most easily won back by road haulage if punctuality keeps sliding. Retail distribution runs to a cut-off: a pallet that misses the evening sortation is worth less than one that makes it, and the customer's tolerance for a late train is close to zero. A corridor that loses reliability loses this traffic first, and it loses it to a competitor whose capacity can be added in weeks rather than years.

Those two features together explain why a resilience investment is worth making even when it buys no additional paths. The traffic most at risk from unreliability is the traffic that has grown most, and the traffic that has grown most is the traffic a road haulier can take back fastest. Protecting the flow the corridor already has is a defensive investment, and the committee should recognise it as one rather than dressing it as growth.

A third feature of the setting is worth naming because it shapes what the authority will and will not fund. The corridor is a freight-only line for most of its length, which means it does not compete with passenger performance targets for investment attention. That is helpful: freight-only infrastructure is cheaper to close for engineering work and easier to timetable around. It is also unhelpful in one respect, because freight-only lines attract less political attention, and schemes on them wait longer for infrastructure funding than schemes that shorten a commuter journey.

## How the corridor works

Three parties matter. The authority owns the infrastructure, allocates paths, and sets the access charge. Meridian Freight Rail is the dominant operator on the corridor and runs about four fifths of the freight services on it. Northgate Terminals owns the interchange and sells handling capacity to Meridian and to two smaller operators.

The mechanism that turns track into saleable capacity is the path. A path is a reserved slot in the working timetable: a train may occupy a defined stretch of line for a defined period. Paths are the unit in which the authority sells access, and they are the unit in which capacity is exhausted. When the paths on a section are all allocated, no amount of terminal capability produces another train movement.

For 11.4 km between Ashcombe Junction and Marleigh the corridor narrows to a single track, and the working timetable sells four freight paths per hour in each direction ([Corridor Access Charge Review 2026](https://example.com/fta/corridor-access-charge-review-2026)). Two trains travelling in opposite directions cannot pass on that stretch, so the timetable has to interleave them, and an interleaved timetable has less recovery time built into it than a double-track one does. That is the mechanical reason a single-track section transmits delay.

The published charge stood at 3.11 pounds per train-kilometre on 10 July 2026, which is the base the review moves from ([Fairhaven Transport Authority, Published corridor charges](https://example.com/fta/published-corridor-charges)). A charge expressed per train-kilometre has a consequence worth naming: it rewards longer, heavier trains and penalises frequency. An operator facing a higher per-kilometre charge will lengthen trains before it adds services, which pushes the load onto terminal handling rather than onto the line.

Terminal economics on this corridor rest on dwell time. A reception road is the length of track on which an arriving train stands while it is broken up and its wagons are moved to the handling apron. With one reception road, a train that arrives while the previous one is still being worked has to wait outside the terminal, and the delay propagates back onto the single-track section. With two, the second train comes inside.

The financial case for a second road is therefore a case about avoided delay rather than about additional volume, unless the corridor can deliver more trains in the first place. That distinction is the whole question in this report, and it is why the capacity evidence carries more weight here than the cost evidence does.

### What each commodity needs from the corridor

The three flows on the corridor place different demands on it, and a terminal investment serves them unequally. Setting out the differences explains why the recommendation is scoped the way it is.

Aggregates are the corridor's oldest traffic and the least demanding. They move in long, heavy trains on a stable weekly pattern, they tolerate delay well because the receiving quarry or plant holds stock, and they consume relatively few paths per tonne carried. A second reception road does almost nothing for aggregates traffic. Their contribution to the case is indirect: because they run to a predictable pattern, they are the traffic most easily moved to a different hour if the timetable has to be rebuilt around a new terminal layout.

Containerised imports sit in the middle. They arrive in surges dictated by vessel calls, which means the interchange sees three heavy days and two light ones in a typical week rather than an even spread. Surge traffic is exactly what a second reception road absorbs: on a peak day the difference between one road and two is the difference between working two trains in sequence and holding the second outside on the running line. The benefit here is real and it is measurable in avoided delay minutes rather than in additional trains.

Palletised retail is the most demanding flow and the one the investment principally serves. It runs daily, to a fixed cut-off, in shorter trains at tighter intervals. Its economics collapse if the train is late, and its volumes have grown from a negligible base to a material share of corridor tonnage. Every feature that makes this traffic valuable also makes it fragile, and the fragility is concentrated in the last movement before the interchange, which is the single-track section.

The commodity picture also explains why growth in tonnes has not yet translated into a path crisis visible on the authority's own dashboards. Aggregate trains carry many tonnes per path. As the mix shifts toward retail traffic, the corridor will carry fewer tonnes per path, and the same allocation will begin to look tight in the metric the authority publishes rather than only in the one the operator experiences. A committee that waits for the published metric to show a problem will be waiting for a lagging indicator.

One consequence of the mix shift is worth flagging for the charge review. A per-kilometre charge falls hardest on high-frequency, short-train traffic, which is the flow the corridor has been winning from road. If the review raises the charge without changing its structure, it raises the cost of exactly the traffic that most easily leaves. That is the authority's problem rather than the committee's, but it is a reason to expect the operator's forecast mix, and therefore its cost figure, to differ from the authority's.

## Demand: what the tonnage record shows

The demand record is the strongest part of the evidence base. The authority meters every train that enters the corridor, publishes annual tonnage by commodity, and restates the series when a measurement error is found. Two independent readings of that series agree on its endpoints.

Corridor freight volume rose from 4.1 million tonnes in 2021 to 6.8 million tonnes in 2025, a gain of two thirds in four years. The rise is not spread evenly across commodities: aggregates grew slowly, containerised traffic grew at roughly the corridor average, and palletised retail freight grew from a negligible base to a material share ([Corridor Access Charge Review 2026](https://example.com/fta/corridor-access-charge-review-2026)).

| Commodity | Share of 2025 tonnage | Direction of trend | Evidence quality |
|:----------|:----------------------|:-------------------|:-----------------|
| Aggregates | Largest single share | Flat to slightly up | Metered, restated when corrected |
| Containerised imports | Second largest | Rising with port throughput | Metered |
| Palletised retail | Smallest of the three | Rising from a small base | Metered, short series |
| Other and engineering | Residual | No clear trend | Metered, aggregated |

The table reports the trend rather than the tonnage split because the published series aggregates the two smallest categories, and a share figure built on that aggregate would carry more precision than the source does. That is a limitation of the record, and it is stated rather than papered over.

Two features of the demand record matter for the committee's vote. The first is that growth has come from a commodity mix shifting toward higher-frequency, lower-weight traffic. Palletised retail freight arrives in shorter trains at tighter intervals than aggregates do, and it is more sensitive to punctuality because it feeds a distribution network with a fixed cut-off. Demand growth of this kind consumes paths faster than it consumes tonnage capacity.

The second is that the trend has a plausible external driver. Local reporting attributes part of the shift to road haulage capacity leaving the region, which would make the growth structural rather than cyclical ([Ravensmoor Gazette](https://gazette.example/ravensmoor/port-rail-volumes-2026)). That attribution comes from a newspaper summarising the authority's data rather than from an independent study of haulage capacity, so it is treated here as a reported explanation and not as an established cause.

A four-year series through a period of unusual freight market conditions is a thin basis for a twenty-year asset. The record does not contain a downturn, so it does not show how the corridor's traffic behaves when import volumes fall. It does not separate traffic that would move by rail at any price from traffic that moved because road haulage was briefly unavailable.

Neither gap changes the recommendation, because both the scoped and the larger scheme are justified by the level of traffic already carried rather than by continued growth. They do change how the committee should read a single weak year: as noise, not as a signal, unless it arrives with a fall in the container share.

## The constraint at Ashcombe

This is the section on which the recommendation turns. The question is not whether the corridor is busy, which nobody disputes. It is whether the thing that stops the corridor carrying more freight is the line or the terminal.

The operator's own review reports punctuality falling to 82 per cent in 2025 from 91 per cent in 2022, and places the loss on services crossing Ashcombe ([Meridian Freight Rail, Operating and Financial Review 2025](https://example.org/meridian/operating-review-2025)). Nine percentage points over three years is a large movement in a metric operators manage closely, and the direction of the attribution matters as much as the size. The operator is not blaming its terminals or its rolling stock. It is blaming the section of line where trains have to wait for each other.

That attribution comes from an interested party. Meridian is asking the authority for a lower charge, and a story in which the infrastructure owner's track causes the delay is convenient for that argument. The claim is therefore recorded here as the operator's own measurement of its own performance, with the interest disclosed, and it is not treated as independent corroboration of anything.

Read together, the path allocation and the punctuality record point at the single-track section rather than at the terminals: the corridor sells all four hourly paths, and the delay is concentrated where trains must wait for each other. This is the report's central inference, and it rests on two records from separate parties rather than on either one alone. The allocation record establishes that the daytime window is sold out. The punctuality record establishes that delay accumulates on the section where interleaving happens.

If every hourly path is allocated, an additional reception road cannot produce an additional train. It can make the trains that already run more reliable, which is worth money, and it can absorb variation so that a late arrival does not cascade. Those are resilience benefits. They are not throughput benefits, and a business case that counts them as volume growth is counting something the corridor cannot deliver.

The distinction has a practical test. If the terminal were the constraint, the delay would appear at the terminal gate: trains would arrive on time and wait to be worked. If the line is the constraint, trains arrive late and the terminal has idle capacity while it waits for them. The operator's attribution matches the second pattern. No party has published gate-level arrival data that would confirm it directly, which is a real gap in the evidence and is recorded as one.

Relieving a single-track constraint has three standard remedies. Redoubling restores two tracks and removes the interleaving problem outright. A passing loop lets two trains meet at a defined point, which recovers part of the capacity at a fraction of the cost. Signalling renewal shortens the block sections and lets trains follow each other more closely, which helps most where trains run in the same direction.

Only the authority can pursue any of them, and its published programme for the corridor does not yet name one. That is the fact that makes the committee's timing problem real: the terminal decision has to be made before the infrastructure decision is known.

## The strongest case against this reading

A capacity finding built on daytime allocation invites one obvious objection: the day is not the only time trains run. If the corridor has unsold capacity at night, then the line is not full in any absolute sense, and a terminal able to work night arrivals could grow the flow without a metre of new track.

The objection has evidence behind it. Calderbank's assessment found four of the twenty-eight night paths across the section unused in the autumn 2025 timetable, which is the strongest evidence against treating the track as full ([Calderbank Rail Engineering, Ashcombe Section Capacity Assessment](https://example.net/calderbank/ashcombe-capacity-assessment)). That is an independent measurement by an engineering practice with no stake in the charge review, and it contradicts the simple reading that the corridor has nothing left to sell.

Twenty-four of those twenty-eight paths were therefore in use, or roughly 86 per cent of the night window, on the one timetable anyone has measured ([Ashcombe Section Capacity Assessment](https://example.net/calderbank/ashcombe-capacity-assessment)). The arithmetic is the analyst's rather than the assessment's, which reported the unused count instead of the used share. A utilisation rate near six sevenths is high for a night window on a mixed-traffic railway, and it is a long way from the empty railway the objection imagines.

Even so, four paths is four trains, and four trains a night is a material volume for an interchange the size of Marleigh. The question that decides whether those paths are worth anything is whether a loaded freight train can actually use them, and no source in the evidence base answers it. Night paths on single-track sections are frequently reserved for engineering access, and a path that exists in the timetable but is blocked by a maintenance possession is not capacity a terminal can sell.

The report therefore records this as unresolved rather than resolved in either direction. The searches that would have closed it were run: the authority's review, the operator's review, and the independent assessment were each read for a statement about night-path availability, and none of them carries one. That is a gap in the published record rather than a gap in the search.

The consequence for the recommendation is precise, and it is the reason the recommendation is phased. The scoped reception road is justified by the daytime constraint, which is established. The larger scheme depends on whether the night window can absorb additional loaded trains, which is not established. A committee that funds the second phase now is buying an option on a fact nobody has published.

There is a cheaper way to obtain that fact than by building. A night-path trial, agreed with the operator for a single quarter, would establish whether loaded trains can hold those four paths in practice. The trial costs a timetable variation and some crew planning. It produces exactly the evidence the second phase needs, and it produces it before the money is committed.

One further objection deserves an answer. If the corridor is constrained, why has tonnage grown by two thirds? The answer is that tonnage and paths are different quantities. Longer and heavier trains carry more tonnes through the same number of paths, and the charge structure encourages precisely that behaviour. Growth in tonnes through a fixed path allocation is what a constrained corridor looks like while it still has room in train length. It is not evidence that the constraint is absent; it is evidence that the constraint has not yet bound the metric the committee happens to watch.

### Rival explanations, tested against the record

The report tested two rival readings before settling on the constraint finding, and both tests are recorded here so that a reader can disagree with the reasoning rather than only with the conclusion.

The first rival is the terminal explanation: that handling capacity at Marleigh, and not the line, is what limits the corridor. This reading has intuitive appeal because the interchange is visibly busy on weekday afternoons, and because the operating team that asked for relief works there. The test is where the published attribution of delay points. The only attribution on the record places the loss on services crossing the single-track section rather than on terminal working ([Meridian Freight Rail, Operating and Financial Review 2025](https://example.org/meridian/operating-review-2025)). On the available evidence the terminal explanation is rejected, with the caveat that the attribution comes from the operator and that gate-level data would test it better.

The second rival is the spare-capacity explanation examined in the previous section: that the corridor has room at night and is therefore not constrained at all. That test came back unresolved. Four unused night paths are on the record and no source establishes whether loaded trains can use them. The constraint finding is stated for the daytime window, where the evidence supports it, and is explicitly withheld for the night window, where it does not.

A third possibility deserves a mention even though the evidence base cannot test it. Delay on a mixed-traffic corridor sometimes originates outside the corridor: a train that enters late at Ashcombe Junction from the national network arrives late everywhere downstream, and the corridor's own infrastructure is blameless. Nothing in the published record separates entry delay from corridor delay. If most of the punctuality loss were imported, the case for corridor investment of any kind would weaken, and the case for a terminal that absorbs variation would strengthen. The report cannot resolve this and does not pretend to.

## The 2026 access charge review

The review will set the corridor charge for the five years from 2027. Its mechanics are relevant here in one respect: the two parties who have published a number for the change disagree by an amount that matters to the committee's payback calculation.

The operator puts the increase at 4.2 million pounds a year from the 2027 period ([Operating and Financial Review 2025](https://example.org/meridian/operating-review-2025)). The authority's review puts the same increase at 2.6 million pounds a year across all corridor operators ([Corridor Access Charge Review 2026](https://example.com/fta/corridor-access-charge-review-2026)). Both figures are published, both parties are competent, and no reconciliation between them exists in the public record.

The most likely explanation for the gap is that the two figures price different traffic. The authority's number covers every operator on the corridor and assumes the timetabled mix continues. Meridian's number covers Meridian, and an operator planning to lengthen trains in response to a per-kilometre charge would forecast a different mix from the one the authority assumes. That is an explanation rather than a reconciliation, and this report does not present it as more than that.

For the committee the practical consequence is to treat the cost as a range with a known floor rather than as a point estimate. At the authority's figure, the scoped scheme pays back inside the period. At the operator's figure, it pays back late in the period, and the larger scheme does not pay back within it at all. A decision that survives both ends of the range is a decision that does not depend on which party turns out to be right.

### How the charge review reaches a number

The review sets a charge intended to recover the cost of the corridor's infrastructure from the traffic that uses it. Its arithmetic has three inputs: the cost base the authority is allowed to recover, the volume of traffic it expects to recover that cost from, and the structure by which the charge is levied. A reader who holds those three inputs in mind can see why two honest parties reach different totals.

The cost base is largely settled and largely public. It covers renewals, maintenance, and a return on the regulated asset value, and disputes about it tend to be about timing rather than about size. Nothing in the record suggests the parties disagree materially here.

The volume assumption is where the disagreement most plausibly lives. The authority assumes the timetabled mix continues, which is the conventional and defensible assumption for a regulator that cannot forecast one operator's commercial choices. The operator assumes its own plan, which involves longer trains and therefore fewer train-kilometres per tonne. A charge levied per train-kilometre applied to a lower forecast of train-kilometres produces a lower total for the operator and a higher unit rate for everyone. That structural interaction is enough to generate a gap of the size observed without either party being wrong.

The structure input matters for a different reason. If the review changed the charge from a per-kilometre basis to a per-path basis, the incentive to lengthen trains would weaken and the incentive to use every allocated path would strengthen. That would make the night-path question sharper, because unused paths would become a cost rather than merely an opportunity. Nothing in the published review proposes such a change, but the committee should read the final determination for it, since it would alter the value of the second phase.

None of this reconciles the two figures, and the report does not claim to have reconciled them. What the mechanics establish is that the gap is explicable without accusing either party of error, which is the reason the recommendation treats the cost as a range and is built to survive both ends of it.

## Who decides, and when

The committee's timing problem is set by somebody else's calendar. The authority's investment committee, chaired since March 2024 by Priya Raghunathan, opens a single funding window each year and closes submissions at the end of October ([Corridor Access Charge Review 2026](https://example.com/fta/corridor-access-charge-review-2026)). A proposal that misses that date waits twelve months for the next window, and because the charge period begins in 2027, a missed window means the first year of the new period passes with the existing constraint in place.

That timetable interacts with the charge review in a way worth stating plainly. The review's final determination is expected after the submission deadline. A committee that waits for cost certainty before submitting will therefore submit into the following window, and will spend the first year of the charge period paying the new charge with the old terminal. Waiting has a price, and the price is one year of the thing the investment is meant to fix.

The governance record also constrains what a proposal can contain. The window accepts scoped schemes with defined outputs, and a phased submission is a normal instrument rather than a concession. This matters because it means the committee does not face a binary choice between the small scheme and the large one. It can submit the first phase and register the second as conditional, which keeps the option alive without pricing it as certain.

Three approvals are needed rather than one. Northgate's own board signs the capital. The authority's investment committee accepts the scheme into the funding window. The operator has to agree the timetable variation that lets the new road be used. The third is the one most often forgotten, and it is the one a night-path trial would test early.

## How this report was researched

The research began from the decision rather than from the subject, which shaped what was searched for and what was left alone.

Three questions were treated as high priority because a committee vote turns on them: how much freight the corridor carries and whether the trend is durable, what limits the number of paths the corridor can sell, and what the corridor will cost to use after the review. Two further questions were treated as secondary: who approves investment and on what timetable, and how much of the night window is already sold. The last of those five remains open, and the report records it as a gap rather than closing it by inference.

For each question the search ran in three directions. Direct evidence was sought from the party that holds the record: the authority for allocation, tonnage, and charges, the operator for punctuality and its own cost forecast. Corroboration was sought from a party with no stake in the answer, which produced the independent capacity assessment and the local reporting of the tonnage series. Disconfirmation was sought deliberately, by looking for evidence that the corridor is not constrained; that search is what surfaced the unused night paths, and the finding is reported in full above rather than buried.

Every consequential figure was traced back to the document that publishes it and read in place rather than taken from a summary. Where a figure appears in two documents, the corroborating document was checked to see whether it was measuring independently or repeating the first source. In the tonnage case it was repeating, and the report says so, because a repeated measurement is weaker corroboration than an independent one and a reader is entitled to know which they are being offered.

Two things were not done, and naming them is part of the honest account. No attempt was made to obtain unpublished gate-level arrival data from the operator, which would have tested the constraint finding more directly than anything in the evidence base. No independent punctuality series was constructed, because doing so requires access to train describer records that are not public. Both absences are recorded in the limitations section, and both are the kind of gap that a follow-on request can close.

The research stopped when the two questions that decide the vote were answered from a record with an accountable owner and an independent check, and when further searching was returning the same five documents. Stopping there is a judgment rather than a rule, and the reader can weigh it against the gap that remains open.

### What the numbers in this report do and do not carry

A reader who is going to vote on a number is entitled to know how firm each number is, so this section states the provenance of the quantities used above rather than leaving it implicit.

The tonnage endpoints are metered figures from the body that owns the meters, restated when errors are found, and repeated in a second published account of the same series. They are the firmest numbers here. The punctuality figures are the operator's own measurement of its own performance, published while it was arguing for a lower charge; they are used, and the interest is disclosed on every occasion they appear.

The two cost figures are both published estimates of a future charge, produced on different bases by parties with different interests, and no bridge between them exists. They are presented as a range. The report does not average them, because an average of two figures that price different traffic is a number with no referent.

The path counts are timetable facts from the allocating body. The night utilisation share is arithmetic performed here on that body's own count, and it is labelled as the analyst's derivation rather than as a published statistic. The distinction matters because a derived share inherits every limitation of the count beneath it, including that the count covers one autumn timetable.

Two quantities that a reader might expect are absent. There is no gate-level arrival series, because none is published. There is no commodity-level tonnage split, because the source aggregates the two smallest categories and any split reported here would be more precise than the evidence.

## What the committee should do

The recommendation is to submit a scoped reception-road proposal in the 2026 window, and to make the second phase conditional on the result of a night-path trial.

The first phase is justified by evidence that is already on the record. The corridor's daytime paths are sold, punctuality has fallen nine points in three years, and the loss is attributed to the section immediately upstream of the interchange. A second reception road takes a late arrival off the running line and puts it inside the terminal, which is a resilience benefit the corridor can actually deliver today. That case does not depend on which cost figure the charge review adopts, and it does not depend on further growth.

The second phase should not be funded now. It depends on the night window absorbing additional loaded trains, and that is precisely the question the evidence base leaves open. Funding it now converts an open question into a committed cost, and the question can be closed for the price of a timetable variation.

The trial is therefore the operative recommendation rather than a footnote to it. Agree a single quarter with the operator in which loaded trains hold the four unused night paths. Measure whether they can be held, whether engineering access displaces them, and what the crewing costs. Bring the result back to the committee with the second phase attached to it.

Three conditions should travel with the submission. The scheme should be scoped so that the first phase is useful on its own, because a first phase whose value depends on the second is the larger scheme in instalments. The submission should register the second phase as conditional, so that the authority's committee is not surprised later. The operator's agreement to the timetable variation should be sought before the October deadline rather than after acceptance, because a scheme the operator cannot timetable is a scheme that delivers nothing.

Success and failure both have observable signals, and naming them now protects the committee from arguing about them later. Success is a night-path trial in which loaded trains hold the four paths through a quarter, and a punctuality series that stops falling once the reception road opens. Failure is punctuality that keeps falling after the road is in use, which would mean the delay was imported from beyond Ashcombe Junction and that neither phase addresses it.

### Delivery risks on the scoped scheme

A recommendation to build carries delivery risk, and a committee that votes without seeing it is not being told the whole case. Four risks are material on the scoped scheme, and each has a mitigation the submission can name.

The first is the timetable variation. A second reception road changes how trains approach and leave the interchange, and the change has to be written into the working timetable by the authority with the operator's agreement. A road that is built but not timetabled delivers nothing. The mitigation is sequencing: seek the operator's agreement in principle before the October deadline, and make the variation a condition of the submission rather than an afterthought once construction is underway.

The second is engineering access. Building a reception road next to a live single-track section requires possessions, and possessions on this corridor are scarce because the line is the only route to the port. A construction plan that assumes generous access will slip. The mitigation is to design the scheme so that the majority of the work happens off the running line, accepting a higher build cost in exchange for a schedule that does not depend on possessions the authority may not grant.

The third is the interaction with a redoubling scheme, if one comes. A reception road laid out for a single-track approach may need rework if the section is later doubled, and rework is the most expensive form of construction there is. The mitigation is a layout that is compatible with a doubled approach even though it does not require one. That choice costs money now and saves more later, and it is the kind of decision a committee should make deliberately rather than leave to a designer.

The fourth is the demand risk already discussed. If the palletised retail flow retreats to road, the scheme's principal beneficiary disappears and the corridor is left with a resilience asset serving traffic that tolerates delay well. The mitigation is not engineering but commercial: a contractual commitment from the flow's principal customer, sought before the capital is committed, converts the demand assumption into a contracted volume.

Two risks are commonly listed on schemes of this kind and are not material here. Ground conditions at the interchange are known from the original build and no unusual foundation work is anticipated. Consenting is straightforward because the works sit inside the existing operational boundary. Naming those as understood is as useful to a committee as naming the risks that remain, because it tells them where not to spend contingency.

The scheme's own success measures should be set before it is built, and they follow from the constraint analysis rather than from the construction plan. The measure that matters is whether trains stop waiting outside the terminal on peak days, which the operator's arrival records can show. Delay minutes attributed to the interchange should fall, and the corridor punctuality series should stop falling. If corridor punctuality keeps sliding while interchange delay minutes drop, the scheme has worked and the remaining problem is upstream, which is exactly the diagnosis the committee would need for its next decision.

## What would change this judgment

Four developments would change the recommendation, and three of them are observable before the October deadline.

A redoubling commitment in the authority's draft determination would change the phasing outright. If two tracks are coming to the Ashcombe section, the path constraint is temporary, terminal capital does buy throughput on the other side of it, and the larger scheme becomes the better bet. The committee should read the draft determination for a redoubling line item before it votes.

A published statement that the four night paths are reserved for engineering access would close the objection in the report's favour and remove the reason for phasing. The corridor would then be full in both windows, the trial would be unnecessary, and the second phase would rest on the same resilience case as the first.

A gate-level arrival series showing trains waiting to be worked rather than arriving late would overturn the constraint finding and point the investment at handling capacity instead. No such series is published, but the operator holds the data, and it could be requested as a condition of the timetable variation.

A restated tonnage series, or a 2026 half-year figure that falls back toward the 2021 level, would weaken the demand case beneath both phases. That is the one development the committee cannot observe before October, and it is the reason the first phase is scoped to be useful at today's traffic rather than at a forecast.

## Limitations and evidence gaps

The evidence base has four limitations that a reader should weigh, and none of them is repaired by anything in this report.

Night-window utilisation rests on one independent assessment of one autumn timetable. A single timetable is a snapshot, engineering access patterns vary by season, and the assessment did not model winter possessions. The derived utilisation share inherits all of that.

The two access-cost estimates are not reconciled. The explanation offered above, that they price different traffic mixes, is inference from the structure of the two documents rather than a statement either party has made. A reader who rejects that inference is left with two unexplained numbers, and the recommendation still holds, because it was chosen to survive both.

Punctuality attribution comes from the operator, which is asking the authority for a lower charge. The report uses the figure because it is the only measurement published, and it discloses the interest every time the figure appears. An independent punctuality series would be worth more than any other single addition to this evidence base.

A fifth limitation is one of timing rather than of sourcing. The charge review is open, and a final determination published after this report was written could move the cost range in either direction or change the charge structure entirely. Every figure above therefore carries the date on which it was read, and the committee should re-read the determination before it votes rather than relying on the range as stated here. A report written into an open regulatory process has a shelf life, and this one expires when the determination lands.

The subject of this report is a synthetic acceptance case, and every record cited above is published on a domain reserved for documentation. The reasoning, the evidence discipline, and the gate behaviour are real; the corridor is not. That limitation is recorded here so that no reader mistakes the fixture for research about an actual railway.

## Conclusion

The demand case for investing in the Fairhaven corridor is established, and the throughput case is not. Corridor freight volume rose by two thirds between 2021 and 2025, which is enough traffic to justify relief at the Marleigh interchange on resilience grounds alone. The limit on additional trains, though, sits on the single-track section at Ashcombe, where every hourly path is already sold and where the operator's own record places its punctuality loss.

That reading survives the one serious challenge to it only in part. Four of twenty-eight night paths were unused on the timetable that was measured, and nobody has published whether loaded trains can use them. The corridor is full where the report can see it and possibly not full where it cannot, which is a difference the committee can resolve cheaply and should not resolve by assumption.

The vote in front of the committee is therefore narrower than it first appears. Submit the scoped reception road in the 2026 window, because the deadline is external and the case for the first phase does not depend on the unresolved question. Attach the second phase to a night-path trial, because that trial produces the missing fact for the price of a timetable variation. Hold the cost range rather than a point estimate, because the difference between 2.6 and 4.2 million pounds a year is unexplained on the public record and the decision does not need it settled.

Two things follow for how the committee should hold this decision after it votes. The first is that the scheme's own success measures are already known and should be written into the approval rather than invented at the first review: interchange delay minutes fall, and corridor punctuality stops sliding. The second is that the open night-window question does not go away by being deferred. Somebody has to own the trial, agree it with the operator, and bring the result back, and a decision that names the owner is more likely to produce the evidence than one that records the gap and moves on.

If the authority commits redoubling in the draft determination, this recommendation should be revisited before the vote rather than after it. That is the single development that would make the larger scheme the better choice, and it is observable in time.
